source: Altitude by the Tangent
Stand a measured distance from the pad, sight the rocket at its highest point, and the tangent of the angle times the baseline gives its height.
Students use sine instead of tangent, or leave the calculator in radians.

From the story. To know how high their rocket went, the boys needed a way to measure height without climbing the sky. Hickam's account says they built their own theodolites, angle-measuring sights, and used trigonometry to estimate altitude. (More in October Sky.)

Here is the idea. Measure a baseline $b$ along the ground from the launch pad to where you stand. When the rocket reaches its highest point, sight it and read the angle of elevation $\theta$ above level. If the rocket went straight up, the pad, you and the rocket make a right triangle. The baseline is the side next to the angle; the height is the side opposite it.

$$\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{h}{b} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad h = b\tan\theta.$$ Add the height of the instrument above the ground. To find the angle to expect: $\theta = \tan^{-1}(h/b)$.
The tracker follows the rocket up. Try a short baseline and a long one with the same height: the angle changes, but $b\tan\theta$ comes out the same.

NASA's classroom version of this uses a hand-held tracker at a fixed baseline (30 m in their activity), adds the height of the person holding it, and averages readings from more than one station. How long a baseline to choose is the subject of the next lesson.
The tangent grows slowly at first and then without limit near $90^\circ$: at steep angles a small misreading makes a big difference in height.
A tracker $200\ \text{m}$ from the pad, with the sight $1.5\ \text{m}$ above the ground, reads $58^\circ$ at apogee. How high was the rocket?
A theodolite reading
$\approx 322\ \text{m}$
$h = 200\tan 58^\circ = 200(1.600) = 320\ \text{m}$ above the sight.
Add $1.5\ \text{m}$: about $322\ \text{m}$, or roughly $1{,}050$ feet.
A rocket should reach about $400\ \text{m}$. A tracker stands $250\ \text{m}$ from the pad. At what angle should they expect it?
Where to look
$\approx 58^\circ$
$\theta = \tan^{-1}1.6 \approx 58^\circ$.

Using sine instead of tangent: $\sin\theta$ is opposite over the hypotenuse, the slanted sight line, which nobody measured. Also check the calculator is in degrees: in radians mode, $\tan 58$ comes out near $8.4$, which makes no sense for this triangle.
